samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Stanley S. Lane was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Okay. You can go ahead any time, Pete.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Hello. This Peter Bartis (ph) from the Veterans History Project. I'm here today with Mr. Stanley Lane. Also accompanying him is Bruce Lane, his son; Keith Wells is the cameraman; and Ms. Virginia Sorkin (ph) from the Library of Congress Veterans History Project, my colleague. We're here at the Marriott Bedford Court in Silver Spring, Maryland, and the date is December 13th, 2001. How do you do, Mr. Lane? I'd like to --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: How do you do?

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: I'd like to begin the interview by asking you to tell me where and when you were born.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: I was -- I was born in Warsaw, Poland, in the Jewish ghetto. And the date I think I gave you, October 1, 1901.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And when did you come to the United States?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: We came here approximately April the 8th, 1908, on the good ship Mauritania.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Really. Do you recall -- when do you recall hearing about World War I?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, after I was here and went through the -- the eight grades in the school and -- well, the war broke out in 1914, and we read a lot about it in the paper. And in 1917, I was 16 years old exactly, and I enlisted in October 19 -- October 17th, 1917. I was exactly 16 years old.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: What did your family think of your enlisting?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, they didn't know about it until later on, after I -- I didn't tell them I was going. And, well, I don't know. Maybe my brother knew, but I went without telling anybody. I didn't want anybody to know I was going to do such a thing, because they wouldn't approve of it, which they didn't. Later on they -- I think they got the Red Cross to get me out. And the Red Cross did come with a service of some kind while I was in Texas, saying that I could get a discharge if I wanted it. And I refused to take it. So we just stayed there to finish things out. I enlisted in the cavalry, and I thought that was the greatest thing going because I'd get a horse and maneuver on horse. And a great deal of my reading books in the library, I read a great many of them by Zane Grey, who was the author of a lot of these scouting books. And I thought that was the greatest thing. I could be a scout. I could learn that and be a trooper and something else. Well, I did. They sent me to the -- Fort Oglethorpe was my first assignment. And there, that's the home -- that was the home of the 11th Cavalry. But at that time they broke it up, and they formed the 22nd Cavalry and the 23rd Cavalry. So I got into the 22nd, and I was in headquarters troop of the 22nd Cavalry. And, well, we just stayed there about six months or so, and then they moved the whole business down to Texas, to a place called China Springs. It's a little town outside of Waco. We stayed there for about six months or so. And then during that time, they changed us to field artillery, horse-drawn field artillery. I was in Headquarters Battery of the 80th Field Artillery at that time. And then from there we went to Fort McClellan, Alabama. Now, we're supposed -- the reason we went there, I think, was to get some training in mountain-type artillery practice, which we did some of it there.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Was this horse-drawn artillery?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Was this horse-drawn artillery?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yes, horse-drawn artillery. And I had a horse. We did a lot of riding.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Had you been on a horse before you joined?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Never saw a horse before. But I enjoyed it. I liked it.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And you were, what, 17?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: As I say, from reading all these books about horses, I thought it was the greatest thing to do.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: What other training did you get when you joined? What other training did you receive when you were in the army?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, nothing in particular, except what the regular enlistees get, which doesn't amount to much or didn't at that time. The only one thing I did get, though, when I was -- and part of this training I got, I got a training which was called the Blue Devils, which was monitored by the French. We had some French officers telling us what to do, training us in what they called the Blue Devils, which today is like the Rangers today. And we had special training on that, and I was a part of that.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Were you expecting to go overseas?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Oh, yes. But I didn't go. I can tell you why.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: I'd like to hear that.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: The reason I didn't go overseas is because it was -- a requirement of going overseas was that I would be a citizen, and I was not a citizen at that time. So during our time in Alabama, when we were scheduled to go overseas, they brought in a federal judge there to grant citizenship to anybody who wanted it. Well, in my instance, all I remember is -- is about 15 or 20 of us came there to go before this federal judge. And they all went there individually, and I suppose they got their citizenship. But when I came there, he said no. So I didn't get any citizenship. And that's why I couldn't go overseas, because there was a law that prevented it. And so then they sent me to another organization that stays in -- that would be in the States.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: What was that?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: And -- I don't know. It was called the Development Battalion. And in there, when I got in there, I became a corporal right away. And I got to be an acting supply sergeant and so on in a relatively few months. I was only 17 years old. But I'll tell you what happened to me there. During our stay there, I, as a corporal, and there's a sergeant was with me and another private was with me, the three of us, we went to -- we took a trip to Birmingham. We were near Birmingham, from Anniston, Alabama, to Birmingham. And so during that period -- it was on a weekend. We left the camp about Friday afternoon and came back on Monday afternoon, all three of us together. And we had some experiences on the way, the car getting stuck in the mud. We hired a driver, and he pulled us. Anyway, when I came back, I was charged with one day of being AWOL. See? Now, actually, I wasn't AWOL at all. I came back on Monday late in the afternoon. We were back in the unit about 4:00 o'clock in the afternoon.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Why did they charge you?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: They charged me. And this is what I say is discrimination. So -- and the reason I say that is because the other two who were with me weren't charged with anything. They weren't even mentioned. I was court-martialled. I was given a summary court and sentenced to 30 days in the jug.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Now, you said it was because of discrimination. What kind of discrimination?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Because -- I say because they court-martialled me. Why didn't they court-martial the other two?

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Do you -- do you know why?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: No. Nothing happened to the other two. They weren't -- anything was done to them. See?

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Why do you think they discriminated against you?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, that's what I don't know. Why did they discriminate against me? Why did they court-martial me? I didn't do anything more than they did.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Well, after this incident passed, what else did you do in the -- what did you do after that?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, let's see. I'm trying to think after that. Nothing. I just went back to duty and got discharged about several months later, when the war was -- the war was practically over then anyway. And, see, going overseas with my unit didn't mean much because by the time they got there, the war was over or it was over the next month, so.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Did you -- did you try to get citizenship again?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Not then and there. When I was discharged, I happened to be in Philadelphia, and I wanted to enlist again in the cavalry.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Why do you think they didn't give you citizenship in Alabama?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Simply because of my name. It's a Jewish name. And my birth name, I must say. It was Samuel Levine to begin with. So I didn't get the citizenship there. But when I came back and was discharged later on, a few months later I went to -- I wanted to reenlist, and I happened to be in Philadelphia. I didn't live there. I just happened to be there. And when I went to the office to enlist, they told me I couldn't enlist unless I was a citizen. So I said -- I went up to the immigration office, and I told them my story. And they said -- and the commissioner, the head man there of the immigration office, said, "You come with me. I'll get you citizenship." And he took me in to a judge, a federal judge, and he swore me in for citizenship. He paid my fee, which at that time was four dollars. I still owe it to him.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Now, what year was that?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: That was in 1919, I guess.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Now, did I -- did you experience part of the flu epidemic while you were in the military?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Oh, that was in 1918, yes.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Could you tell me what that was like?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: When I was in Alabama.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Could you tell me --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: The flu epidemic. All I can remember about that is I apparently had the flu, and they sent me to the hospital. And when I walked into the hospital, the nurse said, "This is your bed over here." And when I walked over there, the -- all these other GIs would stare at me and say, "Hey, the guy that just left there died."

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Greetings to come in there. Because there were a lot of deaths from that flu epidemic in 1918.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: A lot in the military?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: So you got your citizenship and --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, I got my citizenship in 1919, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And then did you reenlist --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Then I reenlisted in the cavalry again. But the cavalry that they sent me to was in Hawaii, of all places. So I started to go to Hawaii.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And still with horses, though?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yes. It was -- the 15th Cavalry was in Hawaii. And I suppose nobody else wanted to go to Hawaii, so. Anyway, I got as far as San Francisco on the trip, and I really don't know what happened, but I was -- something must have happened to me, I don't remember what exactly, that I was placed in the hospital there. The Letterman General Hospital in the Presidio. It doesn't exist anymore today. Oh, I was transferred to the medical corps, and I still was with them for about a year.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And where was that? Was that in California?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yes. In the Presidio of San Francisco, yeah. They sold that whole place to the public there. And while I was there, they sent me -- they sent a cadre of about 15 of us to -- transferred us all to Fitzsimmons General Hospital in Denver. And I was in charge of the cavalry, see. So we went there on the train. And when we got there, I got a job as a clerk to the -- in headquarters. And while I was there, the commanding officer made me a private first class because I established the filing system. See, at that time the Dewey decimal filing system had just come into vogue, and they wanted it there, so I did it for them. I established the decimal system for their office, for the headquarters. So for that he made me a private first class.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Can you tell me what you did before you reenlisted? What did you do in between World War I and your reenlistment in 19 --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, I don't remember exactly, but one of the jobs I had was as a film examiner. I think it was for Fox. We examined the films that came from the movies. The theaters would send their films in after they used them and then they had to be reexamined and replaced re -- or adjusted and so on. And that was part of the job that I had there. It's the only one I can remember. But that was a mean job.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Why do you say that?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, it was a nighttime job. I only worked nights.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: If I could, I'd like to go back to your World War I time and ask you if you have any particular stories that you think of as sad or any experiences that you can recall that were not necessarily the happiest of times. Anything -- anything else happen to you during your first service?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Oh, things were very -- my relationships with my -- the people I had to work with every time was very, very well. It was good. I had no problems with anybody. And I was the signalman for the -- for not in the cavalry, but when we were field artillery, see, we had to have communications.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: So I was the signalman because I knew the semaphore system, and that's about all they had at that time, although radio was coming in and that's why I started in on radio, see. But the radio there was practically useless, because later on I became a radioman, see. I mean, I became what -- a commercial radio operator.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And when was that?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, that was after I -- see, later on when I reenlisted again in 19 -- I don't know, I think -- 23, I enlisted in the cavalry again. And I went to Fort Myer and that was the picture there --

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Fort Myer in Virginia?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: -- at the 3rd Cavalry. Huh?

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: In Virginia?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Fort Myer is in Virginia, yeah. Right outside of Washington here. And while I was there, I -- in that job there at Fort Myer, I was acting sergeant major. I was only a private.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: How did you -- I notice that you increased your rank fairly quickly.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: They didn't -- they didn't give me the rank. They gave me the job.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Major Armstrong, who was the commanding officer there -- and later on, if you ever heard of him, he became deputy to MacArthur as a four star general. He's the one who turned over the surrender of Bataan to the Japanese, see. But anyway, he was a major at the time, and I was his squadron sergeant major acting. But anyway, I held the job down for about six months or so. And I got myself transferred to the Coast Artillery. And in order to transfer to Coast Artillery, I had to pay my own transportation.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: To where?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: To Fort Monroe. You know Fort Monroe, Virginia? And -- well, I did. I think it was -- amounted to something less than three dollars. But anyway, when I came to Fort Monroe, well, I had been in Panama before that, see. I was in Panama in '22, '23. And there's -- I was in the Coast Artillery. That's why I wanted to get back in the Coast Artillery, see.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: When you reenlisted, did you reenlist with the intention of becoming career military?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Not at that time. I didn't have it in mind as a career, but I just liked it, and I wanted to do it. So, I say, I didn't think I was going to make a career out of it. But I -- I just sort of liked that job.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: So you moved around a lot. How did you stay in touch with your family?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Oh, I used to write to them, and I sent them an allotment every time of my -- my pay. I would -- I didn't need anything there. I gave them most of my pay, sent home to my mother.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And where was your mother at that time?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: In New York.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: New York.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: And she needed help a lot, because she had no way of supporting herself. So when I first enlisted, there was 30 dollars a month we got, I sent her 25. I couldn't send her any more. They wouldn't let me, see. There was a limit that you had to have at least five dollars.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: The --

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Hold on, Pete. Let me change batteries.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: When you said -- when you said --

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: I'd like to talk to you about World War II and your experiences during that time. Do you recall where you were on -- during the attack on Pearl Harbor, the Japanese invasion?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Can you tell me where you were and what you were thinking at the time?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, that's going to get -- I'll start from the beginning of when I joined the -- when I reenlisted in the -- or rather, after all those other service, I got out in 1927. I got out, and I stayed out for about six years. During that time I did -- I was in the Connecticut National Guard for a couple of years. And there I was the army mechanic, which was a state job. And I was with them for a couple of years. And after all of that, I --

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Could I ask what work you were doing then? What other work were you doing during that -- those years?

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: What was your civilian work?

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: What civilian work --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, that's what I'm saying. I was the army mechanic.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Oh, the army mechanic. You didn't go far from it. Okay.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah. That was in the -- I was in the National Guard --

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: -- at the same time.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: You had to be in the National Guard to get the job, see. And I came by it accidentally. Actually, I was going to do radio work, because I had graduated the -- see, we skipped. I was in the -- I took a one-year course at the Coast Artillery school in radio engineering, see? So when I got out, I was going to do radio work. So I went to a place that was selling radios and so on, and the fellow that was in charge of that thing was in the National Guard. And he told me, you know, he said, "Why don't you join the Guard?" So when I did, I got the job there as a mechanic. But in the Coast Artillery school, I also took a second course, for another one year, in the mechanical engineering. So I had that behind me. So when I reenlisted in 1933 after staying out six years, in '33 I decided to go back in and stay in. That's when I thought I would stay in.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: That's your third enlistment? That's the third time you went in; right?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah. It's more than that. I was out two or three times. As a matter of fact, I bought out twice. And in those days you could buy out. I don't know as you can do that anymore today. And -- but it was permissible, and I did it.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: How did you buy -- how did you buy out?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, you just tell them, "I want to get out. I got a job here," and get some affidavits saying so-and-so will give me a job for so much per week and so on. And then I had to pay for what they considered the uniform that they had given me. So the first time I did it was 80 dollars and then the next time, a couple years later, it was 120 dollars. That's the buy-out cost. Well, anyway, after I decided in '33, by that time I was married and I had a child. See? And I decided to go back in. I was a -- we skipped off. Well, during the time before I went out in 1927, as a result of going to the schools there in Fort Monroe, the Coast Artillery schools, I became a staff sergeant, which is a -- in those days was a pretty high rank. And so in '33 when I went back, I asked them would they reinstate me to that rank, and they said they would. So I wrote to Washington and got reinstated in '33, went back and had to be on the promotion list. And in about '35, I was promoted to staff sergeant. And shortly after I got promoted, I was sent to Hawaii, which is a nice station.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: What year was that?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: That was in '35.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah, you're right. '38, yeah. I went to Hawaii in '38 and stayed there until August of '40. See, that's just before the Pearl Harbor year.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: And getting to Pearl Harbor, we did -- at that time we did the training in preparation for an attack on Pearl Harbor. And I was a communications officer there. Oh, I skipped something. While I was in the Coast -- first went in the Coast Artillery in '33, I wrote to headquarters in Boston at the First Army and said I wanted to take the examination for a commission. So they sent the papers down and give me an examination. I passed it and got a commission in the reserves. So there I was a commissioned officer in the reserves. So, of course, when I was in Hawaii, I acted as a communications officer, you see, for the harbor defenses of Pearl Harbor, the whole business. And we went through all that training business of going to the different positions where we would set up artillery positions and so on and all the communications we'd have to take. Actually, there I was in charge of a searchlight unit. Let's see. That was one of our main things there, was searchlights to spot airplanes.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Do you think that we were preparing for war then?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yes. Definitely. Because that's what we were training for. And --

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Are you changing it? Hang on a second. And give me a second.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Okay.
[END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE OF TWO; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE OF TWO]

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Ready?

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: I'm rolling.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Let's talk about Pearl Harbor and what you thought about the events that happened.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, as I say, we were in training, and the training consisted of pointing out positions where we would place artillery, because there was only certain places that the enemy could make landings. If you knew the topography of the island, it's mountainous all around. They can't land there very well. So we would put these artillery positions in places where we thought they would land. And in that sort of thing, it was just a matter of training, and weather would be a problem. Now, we knew -- we -- we expected an attack from Japan, yes. But when or how, we didn't know. But later on, of course, we knew. Now, there's one thing about it that I don't know whether this has any substance to it or not. But in the Honolulu paper, I don't remember the exact name of it, there was an advertisement there of certain amounts of -- what would you call -- not dresses, but the parts that dresses are made of.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: These were clothing advertisements?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yes. For women.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: For cloth?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Cloth, a different type of linens or silks and also silk stockings. And if you knew the way -- the way the thing was priced all the way down, there was a system. By the way, this ad was published in this paper and was given to me by a friend of mine from the navy. And they cut it out and clipped it and gave me a copy of it. And it showed there, if you knew the systems, as I say, of how to add up all these prices, that it would come out that the attack would take place on 8:10 Sunday morning, which was the time that it did. And they said that that was put in the paper to warn the Japanese citizens who lived there that it was going to take place.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Interesting.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Those that were supposed to, knew it.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: I know that they were very concerned about sabotage in Hawaii.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Not too much, because as we -- as communications people, we would say if you go out in such-and-such an area and look for a spot that we had planted there, if you can't find it, ask the nearest Jap, he'll tell you where it is.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Now, where was your family --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: They were with me.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: -- when you were in Hawaii? They came with you in Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah. My wife and son was with me.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And your son Bruce?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Could I ask what kinds of things you did in Hawaii outside of the military service?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, we mostly went to the beach. Though, I was an umpire on all baseball games. As a matter of fact, the day I got off the ship, instead of going anywhere even to a house, I went to umpire a baseball game. Because a friend of mine was an umpire there, and when I landed he -- "We need an umpire on bases," so I got the job. So that was one of the things I did there.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: I notice that as we talk that you've taken a lot of opportunities for special training in the military, and that's advanced you forward.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah. Well, that's going to the Coast Artillery school. That's one of the things. The Coast Artillery school was the -- the courses that they set up, they had really three courses. One was radio, the other was electrical, and the other was clerical. Now, the electrical course, which I also took, was set up by a Professor Timbig (ph) from Yale, and he said it was approximately what engineers would have to learn the first year as an engineering course. So I guess we got some pretty good training there in that. As a matter of fact, I worked as an electrical staff sergeant for several years, and in that -- that job, I was in charge of power plants, I ran power plants. See, all these Coast Artillery batteries had to have power plants to operate. And we had 25kw generators to supply all the power to these places and all the batteries, so wherever you went on a Coast Artillery post, you had to have a power plant, so that's what we operated. And that's why we went to that school.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Where were you when the Japanese invaded Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: I was in Massachusetts. I was -- let's see. I was -- oh. Well, by that time I had already been commissioned. Because when I came back from Honolulu, I went to New Bedford to a post there. I don't remember the name of it even.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Fort Rodman. Fort Rodman.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Rodman, yes. Fort Rodman. And so while I was there, the -- let's see, that was in '41.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: When did you hear about the invasion?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: That's what I'm trying to sort of get the right spacing here.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: But you had already come back. You were in Hawaii until 1940?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: In August of 1940, I guess we came back. That's when we went to Fort Rodman, and we stayed there for a while. And -- oh. At that time -- that's what happened. The president declared an emergency. So since he declared the emergency, I went to Boston to the army headquarters and talked to the right people and told them to call me to active service as an officer, which they did, see. That was about a year later. So I was -- I got on active duty as a first lieutenant at Camp Edwards. That's in Falmouth, Mass., on Cape Cod. So --

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: When the attack occurred --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: When the attack occurred, that's where I was.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Yeah. And did you still have friends in Pearl Harbor at the time?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Did I what?

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Did you have friends still living in Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Oh, yes, we had -- we always had -- in the Coast Artillery, we have friends all over the world.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Right. So that must have been a little shocking for you.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: But you expected that attack, though, didn't you?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah, we did. The worst one is friends of mine that I know were the ones in the Bataan march. They were in the Philippines. There was one in particular, friend of mine, was in that march. He died in that thing. And another one is one of the officers was in the Bataan march is in that picture right there.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Well, we'll look at those pictures a little later. We'll talk about those. So did you go overseas in World War II?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah. I was in the first ones.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Where did you go?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: I was -- when -- when I got orders to go overseas, I was assigned as a -- to on Eisenhower's staff. I was a captain at the time. And that was in -- I think in July of '42. Anyway, we were the first -- went over with the first convoy that left the States. It was about eight ships total, eight ships carrying about 5,000 troops. And we were escorted by half of the navy, I think. Anyway, about halfway over, half of the ships got lost and went off somewhere's else. But we landed in -- in England all right with no problems. We got on a railroad. I'm trying to think of the name of the place up north. It's one of their -- I think it's Liverpool, Liverpool area. And they took us by train down to our station. I was supposed to be on Eisenhower's staff, which was in London, but we never got to London. Our headquarters, and it turned out to be the headquarters of everybody at that time, was in -- the name doesn't come to me just now.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Cheltenham? Cheltenham?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Cheltenham, yeah. Cheltenham is the name of the town there. And that's where the entire headquarters was. And Eisenhower never came there, but most everybody else did.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: When you were going over on the convoy, did you sense much danger on that trip?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, they always talked about it, but I don't think we ever ran into any. They always talked about submarines and no airplanes.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: What was -- how long did that trip take?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: About seven days.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Seven days?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah. We were escorted by a lot of destroyers and also a bigger ship. Not a battleship, but a cruiser, I think.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And what did you do while you were in England?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, while I was England I was set up to be at that time called a salvage officer. And I was just on the staff. We were establishing ideas of depots in different places, what we were going to use them for and so on. And I did that for about six months. See, we got over there in July, I guess, or the end of July, and in November I was -- I was sent to the invasion of North Africa. And I was with the first troops to land in North Africa.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And what was your position when you went there?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, I was still the salvage officer, see. And in one of those, I was on the staff of the Second Army Corps. The Second Army Corps was the one that handled it. We had a couple of divisions there.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: What branch --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: The First Division was one of them.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: What branch of service were you in then?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: I was in the quartermaster at that time.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Could you explain what that -- what the quartermaster --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, the quartermaster takes care of all supplies except ordnance or signal, almost everything. Well, I tell you, while I was there, I established a depot there in which we did almost everything to reclaim or re-serve all the items that were used. As an example, we had a shoe repair system. I had a company of soldiers that did nothing but shoe repair and another company that did clothing repair and another one for tent repair, stuff like that. And, of course, then there was typewriter repair and adding machine repair, things of that nature. I was in charge of that whole business, to see that it operated properly.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Was this in North Africa?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: What happened to the ships when you came to -- when you arrived in North Africa?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, when we arrived, nothing happened. There was a couple of ships ahead of us, I think, that got sunk there by the -- by the -- the French.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: By the French?

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: The Vichy French?

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: You said by the French?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah, the French. I forget the name of them they had.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: The Vichy French?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: The Vichy French. What do you call them?

sp.speaker: Virginia Sorkin
sp.p: Vichy.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Vichy French.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Vichy French, yeah. See, they had to battle them for a while. And they sank a couple of ships there, but there wasn't much loss of life on those ships. But I had that with some -- on one of the ships there we had about 50 nurses and WACs. And they lost about all of their clothing and so on. And one of the jobs I had was to go around and ask them, all these women, what sizes, what size clothes they wore and underwear and all that and then go get it for them, see. Because they only had no place to get it except the department stores there. Well, we didn't have much trouble getting them. We could get the things all right, if we knew that they wanted, see.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: How did they lose their clothing?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: On the ships.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: That sunk?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Those ships that were sunk. They rescued these nurses. So that was one of the starting things that we had there.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: What did you do from North Africa? Where did you go after North Africa?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, after North Africa I was sent back to the States again. I came back to the -- my assignment was the 7th Service Command in Omaha, Nebraska. And up there, as I say, I was in the salvage section again. Once you get in that, they will keep you there, I guess. Nobody wants that job.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Why do you say that?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: I don't know. Because it's nothing glamorous about it, see.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: But it sounds very difficult.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, it's a lot of work to it, but nothing that you can write home about, as it were. You're not a hero, see. But anyhow, while I was there, I -- I went to the Commanding General Staff School there, which is Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. Well, I graduated that thing, and then I got a job on the general's staff in 1st Army in New York. So I went back to New York again.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Was your mother still there?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: No. What?

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Was your mother in New York still?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: My mother?

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: You said you had family in New York.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: No, no. My father and mother were long gone by then.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: So you're back in New York, still in the military.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah. I was in the -- stationed at the 1st Army Headquarters, which is on the island there at -- what's the name of the place?

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Governor's Island.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Governor's Island. It doesn't exist anymore. It's been sold to somebody.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: I think they were talking about restoring that place for historic preservation purposes.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: There was some talk about it. I'm not sure if they actually did it. What did you -- you stayed in the army until was it 1955?

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: 1955. What did you do in the ten years you -- were you basically stationed in New York after World War II?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, in New York in the -- I was on the general's staff there. See, I was a quartermaster on the general's staff, and there I served a couple of different things. Part of it was I was advisor to the commanding general on legal matters, and I was no more a lawyer than you are. But anyway, I held the job for about a year. And we had a lot of experiences there with some of the contractors we had. One contractor we had was the one who supplied milk to us from Fort Dix. And one time our laboratory said the milk was contaminated, so we had to cancel his contract. So he called his -- his representative in Washington.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: His Congressman?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: His Congressman, who apparently was a lawyer. I don't know whether he was or not. He got his Congressman to come in and talk to the general there. So we had a session with the commanding general and this Congressman and this guy wanting to know why we were going to cancel his contract. Well, we canceled his contract because the water was contaminated. And we found out, even before this meeting, that the reason it was contaminated was because his brother had tapped into the water line and was stealing water there also that had contaminated the place. So he didn't have much leg to stand on. But anyway, that's one of the things you run into. The other thing I was -- in interest there, I was in charge of precious metals. People from all over the country would send in what they considered precious metals. That was platinum and gold and things like that. And I had a -- I had a room in the army headquarters there to put that stuff in, and then we would auction it off.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Why did -- why did people send this material to you?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, there was a regulation out that they would do that, because they couldn't use it. There were certain -- there were certain things that they used that contained this material, and when that -- when those things broke down or couldn't be repaired, they had those things taken out and shipped to us. And we would sell them on the open market to people who bought and sold gold and silver, things like that.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: That was one of the operations. And one of the bigger operations that I had was we held an auction in Schenectady, New York, in Schenectady depot. There was a depot in Schenectady, and we held an auction there, about seven million dollars' worth of material, and I had to go up there and supervise the thing. And we hired civilian auctioneers to operate the thing. And this was nationwide. People came in from all over the country there to buy some of these things. And I had some pictures of it somewhere, but --

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: If you look back over your -- over your long career in the military, is there any special event that stands out most in your mind?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: I don't know what to pick up, but.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: The -- I notice as I listen, you certainly traveled a lot, and I guess you've moved your family with you in many places?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: How was that? Was that difficult to do?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, it depended, I guess. Most of the time we did it by automobile. For example, when I -- well, we traveled -- from Hawaii we came back by rail. Because that was at government expense, we came all the way from San Francisco to New York by rail, so we had no problem with that. But we also traveled across the country twice, I think, by automobile, mostly at our own expense.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Did you find the army's support services helpful as you traveled from different places or were you pretty much --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, I didn't use them, but you could have. You could stop at any post and use their facilities there for staying overnight or something.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: You might want to talk about your service at Fort Lee. You haven't mentioned Fort Lee at all.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Could you tell me about your service at Fort Lee?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah. Well, at Fort Lee, well, there's one picture there. I was at the quartermaster school there for about six months there. That was the training course. But later on I was -- oh, I was at Fort Lee with the -- the quartermaster school. And I was the department head, the maintenance department. I was in charge of that maintenance department. And there we had classes for all sorts of things, like shoe repair, laundries, dry cleaning, typewriter repair, machines, automatic machines of all kinds. I had classes in all those things. People from all over the country would come in there to those schools. But I had a staff of about eight officers monitoring each one of those courses.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: What was your rank then?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, I was a lieutenant colonel by that time.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: When did you become a lieutenant colonel?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: I think it was in 1950, just about the beginning of the year, see. So from '50 to '55, all those five years I was a lieutenant colonel.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: And that's --

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: That's after --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: -- the whole time I was in the -- around the quartermaster school in that same job.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: That was partially during the Korean War?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yes. During the Korean War that's where I was. And the only thing we did in the Korean War there was to help the French. There was one instance there the French Foreign Legion was surrounded by the Vietnamese, and they couldn't get any supplies in because they didn't have any parachutes, so they asked us for parachutes. And we had to prepare the parachutes for them. We sent them about 300 parachutes. So that was one job we had. It took about a week or so to prepare all these parachutes.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: You were preparing them where?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: We prepared them for shipment, you know.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: You had to fix them so they could be used.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Look at all of them, see that they were in good shape.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: But did you go to Korea ever?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: I wanted to talk to you about your choice of service. Why did you join the army and not another -- when you joined so many times, how come you stayed in the army rather than the navy or --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: -- air force?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, I don't know. I didn't care about joining the navy because I didn't like being aboard ship all the time. But I tried to join the marines once, and they turned me down. They said I had a hernia, which I didn't know anything about. You know, they gave me a physical. So they wouldn't let me enlist because I had a hernia.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Oh --

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: You were going to tell me about your Fort Lee experience when you were quartermaster there.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah. Well, that's the main thing I did there at Fort Lee. See, Fort Lee is the home of the quartermaster, and they have all sorts of activities there. And from there everything springs out all over the country. When you do something, it becomes law around the army.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: We have a few things here that I wanted to ask you about that were brought to my attention. One of them is something to do with this book. I thought maybe you could tell me the story about that.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: This was an operation that I started when I was at Camp Edwards on the Cape. And when I did all of that there, this was salvage operation as they call it. I was a salvage officer, see, and at that time, I was a captain. And we started all these activities. And, see, that was Nashaweena (ph) Mills, the big cotton people. And they had a lot of space there. That was when the -- that sort of business was sort of downhill. So we rented part of their space and started an operation. We had no place on the Cape there to do it, so we had to do it -- I had to get permission from the commanding -- from the Quartermaster General to do this, see. So they gave it to us, and we did it. And there's a lot of write-ups here about how we started and all these people here.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Is that where the Eisenhower jacket was done?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Now, who is that?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: That was me. See?

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Great. Good-looking guy.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: The Eisenhower jacket was made by a friend of mine who was a tailor, and he made it for me. But I didn't get anywhere's with it because in England, when we went to England, I found that somebody else had an Eisenhower jacket made there, so I couldn't in any way get any credit for that. But anyhow, I was the first one, I guess, or nearly the first one to have made an Eisenhower jacket. And I wore it in England. See, that's Mr. Murray and his secretary there. He was the manager of this operation here. See, I couldn't be there because I was at -- I was at Camp Edwards, and this was in New Bedford. So I had to commute all the time. And he was the only one with shoe repair. Now, the big thing about shoe repair was that I was the first one to start using plastic soles for repair of shoes in the army. And when I did that, all the leather people around Boston got angry, and the first thing they did was call their Congressman, see.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: There was a big shoe business there.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: They wanted to know why I didn't I order leather from them. I stopped ordering leather.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Did you use -- did you use plastic or rubber?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Rubber.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Rubber.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah. I called them plastic, but -- and then that's what started everything all over the country, see. Because at that time, I had other reasons, but the shoe soles that we bought in leather at that time cost about a dollar and ten cents or something like that, and the plastic was only about 15 cents, so you see the difference. But one of the main reasons was that on the Cape, see, at that time we were -- the 26th Division from Massachusetts was in there for training, and we had to fix their shoes. But at that time, see, they're on a sandy terrain. And the sandy terrain wears leather out like nobody's business, so that's why we used plastic. So I had a good reason for it and got around it. But anyway, they called their Congressman to find out. And we had in here all the direction --
[END OF SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE OF TWO; BEGIN SIDE ONE, TAPE TWO OF TWO]

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Ready to go.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Mr. Lane, I'd like to ask you one more question before we look at some of the photographs and things that you have here from your military past. I know you read the newspaper and keep up with the news every day, and I would like to hear your perspective on what's going on today in Afghanistan and some of the things that are happening now.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, Afghanistan, their problem of fighting the people who are there is just the same thing as we did in the Vietnam and places like that, fighting in the jungles. It's -- it's a thing that you have to do step by step because you never know when you're going to run into the enemy. There's all sorts of hiding places and get you ambushed a lot, and that's what's happening over there to some degree. And -- but those are chances we have to take. We'll have to have some casualties. There's no question about it. But that's the only way we're going to make any progress in the battle over there, the only way I can see it, in the caves. I would say if we can get close enough, instead of bombing them, we throw in a few canisters of tear gas and then a few hand grenades and that will get them moving.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: That's what they did in Vietnam. Well, of course, you know you witnessed the tragedy in the World Trade Center and the towers coming down. How did you feel when you first saw that? What came -- what was your first thought?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: The first thing was get the whole air force after them and do something about it. It's something that makes your blood boil to see that they could do such a thing. It's crazy. Suicide bombers are crazy. They must be in order to commit suicide over a thing like that. But those people are trained in their religion that if they do things like that, they're going to go to heaven. They haven't found what heaven is like yet or where it is.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Before we look at some of the pictures and things, is there anything -- is there a question that you would have liked me to ask that I didn't ask? Is there something else that you'd like to add.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: No, I can't think of anything at the moment. But as we go through some of these, it may come up.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Okay. Okay. Shall we break?

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Okay. Just give me a second.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Do you want me to move my chair?

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: No, I think I'm okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Let me take some of these --

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Move some of the stuff off the table, probably.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Mr. Lane, I would like to look at a few of these items here and have you tell me about them. I see you have your cap from the service. Could you tell me about this and what this means?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, this is an overseas hat that we got during the war, World War II, and these ribbons all pertain to a particular campaign, and the star on them indicates that there was some action there. And this is World War I. This was -- actually, I'm entitled to a couple more, but I haven't got a medal on there. I have a commendation from a major general, which gives me a commendation medal. That would be another one, see. And there was another one, I forgot what.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Do you remember what each of these are for?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: This -- I don't remember these. This is the Hawaiian campaign. And this is American something. I don't remember. I don't remember what they're for exactly. One of them is -- I don't know. I can't remember them all.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Could you try it on?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Oh, yeah. It fits me all right.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And what's the silver?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: That's the lieutenant colonel's rank insignia.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Let me ask you about a few other things we have here. This one here, what is that?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: This frame, I made that when I was in the hospital for the flu, the flu epidemic.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: In 1918. So they had, you know, craft courses there, so I made that there. And this is a picture of me in -- taken about that same time, so I was about 17 years old there.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And this picture right here?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: That's a picture of me at Fort Myer, Virginia, in the 3rd Cavalry. And this fellow on that horse beside me, his name was Miller. And he's the -- he was the bugler that blew taps at all the funerals and so on. So he was the regimental bugler. And there I was the sergeant major, see, acting.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Now, is that horse --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: This is the headquarters for the -- this is right in front of the headquarters building.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Now, is this horse larger than the other one here?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: No, they're about the same. They're both pretty good horses.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Yeah? Did you have a favorite horse that you kept?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, you were assigned to a horse and usually kept him, if he was any good.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Right. And let me ask you about this, to Lieutenant Colonel Stanley S. Lane.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: See, that's Cleveland Retired Officers Club. When I lived in the Cleveland area, which was from about '56 through '90, '91 or '2, all those years, I started the Cleveland Retired Officers Club. See, and I was the -- see, it says founding president, so I was the first president there. I started the club. In fact, I wrote to all the people to come to a meeting to start up, and they came and had about 30 people come the first meeting. So they gave me that plaque.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: How did you find yourself in Cleveland?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, after I got out of the -- when I retired, I was in -- the first job I had was in Florida. I went down there, stayed there about, oh, eight or nine months. And we came to Cleveland because at that time my son had gotten a job in Cleveland with a law firm. So we came up to Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: So were you active when you were in Cleveland in any of the other veterans' service organizations? Were you a part of the American Legion or --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: No, no. Just this. One of them is enough.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Now, I'd like to ask about this picture here.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: That was taken about a year before I retired at Fort Lee. They took that picture. And that, of course you know, that's what the president sent me for my hundredth birthday.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And your hundredth birthday was on?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: October 1st.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: October 1st.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And this is signed George --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: From President Bush.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: -- Bush. Yeah. That's wonderful. And here's another picture. I'd like you to tell me about it and if you even remember what you were thinking then. It's a lovely picture.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: That's when I first came here. We got off the ship. That's my aunt. She met us to take us to a place where we were going to live, and along the way they took our picture. That's when I first landed. I was about a little over six years old at the time.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Do you remember anything about that trip? That was a long time ago.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: No. The only thing I can remember is when she met us, you know, at Battery Park in New York, that's where the ships land, we got off. We took the Ninth Avenue elevator. There's no more elevator there today. They knocked it down. So we were riding on the elevator with her, and she gave me a banana, which was a great deal in those -- never heard or saw a banana before.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Really. I want to ask you about a couple of other things. And this picture here, are you in this picture?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah. Right there.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Right there.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: My name is down there somewhere. Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And when was -- why was this picture taken? Is this your --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: It's a class picture. This particular, advance supply officers.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And this was at Camp Lee.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Camp Lee, Virginia.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And these are other class pictures that we have too?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: And that's the one at -- that's the Commander General Staff School in Leavenworth.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And this is 1944.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah. See, the 20th General Staff Class.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And here you are right here.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah. That's a pretty big class.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: It sure is.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Anyway, there's all sorts of different rank officers here from captains to colonels and majors. I was a major at the time.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Yes, I see. And there's something else that you've saved.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: And I might also say I graduated near the top of the class.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Oh, you did? I want to ask about this book here. Then can you tell me what's in this book?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: I don't know what's in it. I never saw it before.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Oh, really? I think you've seen everything that's in here. This is your enlistment record?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah. That must be my first discharge, yeah? Yeah. And I don't know --

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: He has not seen this in book form before.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: -- who wrote all that.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: He has not seen this in book form before --

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Oh, not all put together like this?

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: -- because his grandson put this all together for him just recently.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: He did a beautiful job.

sp.speaker: Virginia Sorkin
sp.p: Can you turn to the --

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Virginia Sorkin
sp.p: Can you turn to the one page that has the whole service?

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: There are various other items here. Another enlistment record.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: There's another one.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: So you did enlist a few times.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: There is a page here that we'll come to later that has all of his military service recorded. It's a little bit further back. It will take a second to find it.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: I think we went by it. I think it's coming up.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Here. Is that it?

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Yeah, that's it. That's it.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: This is your statement of service as of February 1954.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Well, we have quite a few documents here. And you've kept all of these or --

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: That's a complete record from his first enlistment in 1917 through to his retirement in 1955.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And what's -- this is -- what is this right here?

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: It's his certificate of retirement.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: It's your certificate of retirement. Were you glad to see that when you got it?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Not particularly.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: I didn't want to retire. Eisenhower made us retire.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: He did?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Would you -- you wouldn't have retired after all those years in the service?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Explain to him how that --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: I liked the service very well.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Explain to him why Eisenhower made everybody retire then. What was the rule?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Eisenhower issued an order that all colonels with 30 years service and lieutenant colonels with 28 years had to retire. And at that time I had 29, so I had to go out. I didn't go out.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Why did he issue that order?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Because I wanted to get 30 years in.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: So I got -- I took my former regular army rank of chief warrant officer, and I took that for about a year to get 30 years in. And then I had to retire. The law required it.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Why did he make that law, do you know why?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: 30 years was something that always came up in different laws. If you had 30 years' service, that was, you know -- I don't know, an earmark or eye mark or whatever you want to call it.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: So you'd be in the military today --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: I wanted to get 30 years.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: So you would be there today, if you could?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Well, thank you, Mr. Lane. This has been a very nice opportunity for me to learn about you and about your military experience.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: And we forgot about this.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Oh, yes. There's one other thing we'd like to look at here. Let me hold this up. Could you tell me --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: This thing, I never --

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And what's the story?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: This is supposed to be a secret jewelry box, see. Now, the thing is -- here it is. It's not -- yeah. See? That comes out.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: And there's supposed to be a catch there. I lost it. So you push it back up.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Who made this for you and where?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: This was made for me by an Italian prisoner while I was in North Africa.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Why did he make this for you?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Just -- I don't know. Just out of friendship or we were treating him right. It took him quite a while, I guess, to make that. It's got all these notations on there. These are various stations I was at at different times.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: And who wrote those on there?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: The person who made this box wrote those on there?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. He did this whole thing. And I think down here it says something also. Just my name, I think.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: It's your name on it.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Yes. Well, thank you very much.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: You okay?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Tired?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: You got your workout.

sp.speaker: Keith Wells
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: That's wonderful.

sp.speaker: Virginia Sorkin
sp.p: It was great. This is very beautiful. And you've kept it all these years.
[INTERRUPTION IN RECORDING]

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Okay. You were saying that --

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Two other soldiers and myself, we took a trip to Birmingham. We were stationed at Fort McClellan, Alabama.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Yeah, you told me about going there.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, we took a trip to Birmingham on Friday afternoon and came back on Monday afternoon. And when we came back, I was charged with one day AWOL. The other two fellows weren't charged with anything. They were all just with me, right all the same time. And not only being charged, I was a corporal at the time. And the punishment for one day AWOL was practically nil.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: But in my case, I say they discriminated against me because of my name --

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: -- at that time, Samuel Levine. They court-martialled me. And the court-martial gave me a 30-day sentence in the guardhouse, which I served. And while I was in there, there was a riot. They turned out a battalion of troops to quiet us down and all that. And there's no reason why they should have court-martialled me and did nothing to the other two guys.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Did you feel like there was much discrimination, being a Jew in the army at that time?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: I didn't. I didn't sense very much, because I got along very well with my fellow soldiers and so on. They didn't bother me at all. And this was the only way, and I don't know. It was -- this was done by officers.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Not by enlisted men.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: But you still went on to have quite a career.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Well, I had to go get a citizenship, which I got later, and it was all right.

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: But that experience didn't embitter you at all?

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: No, it didn't bother me. I had --

sp.speaker: Peter Bartis
sp.p: You just moved on from there. Well, I'm going to close this off.

sp.speaker: Stanley S. Lane
sp.p: Okay.
[END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE TWO OF TWO; END OF INTERVIEW]
